method: Full texts read where open: Clauset et al. 2009 (arXiv 0706.1062, Tables 6.1-6.3), Corral & Gonzalez 2019 (arXiv 1810.07868), Kagan 2010 (arXiv 0908.1207), Utsu et al. 1995 (J-STAGE), Dussauge et al. 2003 (ISTerre PDF), Hack 1957 (USGS), Dodds & Rothman 1999 (arXiv cond-mat/9808244), Papale 2018 (Europe PMC), Mandelbrot 1967 (JSTOR scan), Guzzetti 2006 dissertation ch. 5 (CNR-IRPI). Abstracts via Semantic Scholar / OpenAlex keyless APIs for paywalled papers. PDFs converted with pdftotext and grepped; quotes copied from extracted text (whitespace normalized). All DOIs confirmed via Crossref. Exponent conventions recorded per source and never converted.

rows.item: Earthquake intensities, California 1910-1992 (Clauset data set q)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of the tail of earthquake intensity (maximum amplitude of motion, x10^3)
rows.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), SIAM Review
rows.notes: Table 6.1 row (n = 19 302; xmin 0.794 +/- 80.198; ntail 11 697; power-law goodness-of-fit p = 0.00, so pure power law ruled out at Clauset's p <= 0.1 rule). Variable is amplitude-based intensity, not magnitude or moment, so alpha is not a b-value. Text: power law 'plausible only if one assumes an exponential cut-off'.
rows.convention: PDF exponent alpha, p(x) ~ x^-alpha for x >= xmin (Clauset eq. 1.1); fitted by maximum likelihood with xmin chosen by minimizing KS distance; '1.64(4)' means 1.64 +/- 0.04
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Vuong normalized log-likelihood ratio (Table 6.2; positive favors power law): log-normal -7.14 (p 0.00), exponential 11.6 (p 0.00), stretched exp. -7.09 (p 0.00); nested LR vs power law + exponential cut-off -24.4 (p 0.00). Verdict 'with cut-off'; text says stretched exponential 'strongly favored over the power law' for earthquakes.

rows.item: Seismic moment, southern California catalog
rows.quantity: PDF exponent of seismic moment distribution (untruncated power-law fit)
rows.source: Corral & Gonzalez (2019), Earth and Space Science
rows.notes: Table 1: N = 179,255, fit above 1.5e21 dyn cm (about Mw 3.4) over 5.89 decades, n = 2,883, KS p = 0.30. Table 6 preferred model: untruncated power law. Corral's PDF beta 1.655 corresponds to a CCDF exponent of 0.655 by Corral eq. 2, which is Kagan's beta convention; we do not convert, flagging only that these are different conventions.
rows.convention: PDF exponent beta, f(x) ~ x^-beta (Corral eq. 1; CCDF exponent would be beta-1, not used here)
rows.alternative_test: ML fit + KS goodness-of-fit with Monte Carlo p-value; truncated vs untruncated power law; power law vs truncated log-normal via the logarithmic coefficient of variation (cv_l) test (Malevergne et al. 2011). Untruncated power law preferred.

rows.item: Seismic moment, global CMT catalog
rows.quantity: PDF exponents of the two power-law regimes of global seismic moment
rows.value_text: truncated power law beta = 1.655 for 1.3·10^24 to 2·10^27 dyn cm (p 0.46); untruncated beta = 2.087 above 4.0·10^27 dyn cm (p 0.33, n = 97)
rows.source: Corral & Gonzalez (2019), Earth and Space Science
rows.quote: we find two power-law regimes, the first ranging up to about 7.6 in moment magnitude, with the usual exponent β = 1.655,
rows.notes: Tables 1, 4, 6. N = 48,636. Upper regime 'beta ≃ 2' above about Mw 7.6, fitted on only 97 events. Preferred distribution: double power law. Contrasts with Kagan's tapered Pareto reading of the same catalog (pl-04).
rows.convention: PDF exponent beta, f(x) ~ x^-beta (Corral eq. 1; CCDF exponent would be beta-1, not used here)
rows.alternative_test: Same ML/KS + cv_l protocol: single untruncated power law fits only the top 97 events; truncated power law covers 3.2 decades; log-normal not preferred; final call 'double power law'.

rows.item: Scalar seismic moment, global shallow CMT catalog 1977-2008
rows.quantity: index beta of the (tapered) Pareto distribution of seismic moment
rows.value_text: 0.63–0.67 (catalog estimates); Table 2: 0.6820 global, mt = 5.8, 5450 events; proposed bias-corrected 0.52–0.56
rows.source: Kagan (2010), Tectonophysics
rows.quote: usually yield a value in the range 0.63–0.67, equivalent to the commonly known G-R b-value of 0.95–1.0
rows.notes: Kagan argues upward biases (moment errors, clustering, source complexity, depth) inflate beta, and a theoretical value of 1/2 is plausible. Table 2 also gives 0.6480 (declustered), 0.6463 (subduction zones), mt = 5.6.
rows.convention: CCDF (survivor) exponent: F(M) = (Mt/M)^beta for M >= Mt; tapered form multiplies by exp((Mt - M)/Mc); Kagan states b = (3/2) beta
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Tapered Pareto (power-law body with exponential taper at corner moment) vs pure Pareto; likelihood map in beta x mc; observed CCDF 'clearly bends downward' at large m, tapered form adopted (fig. corner mc = 8.9; only lower 95% limit mc ≃ 8.3 resolved). No log-normal comparison; statistically significant misfit of tapered form at m > 7.8 attributed to catalog methodology.

rows.item: Gutenberg-Richter b-value, global Harvard CMT shallow earthquakes
rows.quantity: b-values of two magnitude-frequency branches (small vs large shallow earthquakes)
rows.source: Sornette, Knopoff, Kagan & Vanneste (1996), Journal of Geophysical Research
rows.quote: the b values are b2 = 2.3 ± 0.3 for large shallow earthquakes and b1 = 1.00 ± 0.02 for smaller shallow earthquakes
rows.notes: Abstract read on arXiv PDF and Semantic Scholar. Crossover magnitude ill-defined: 50% probability between M 7.1 and 7.6.
rows.convention: cumulative magnitude-frequency, log10 N(>=M) = a - bM (b of magnitude distribution derived from moment catalog via rank-ordering statistics)
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Two-branch power law vs single power law via rank-ordering statistics; authors caution there is 'no direct evidence' the large-moment branch is a power law and that a gamma distribution (power law with exponential tail) fits the whole moment range satisfactorily.

rows.item: Gutenberg-Richter b-value, southern California catalog
rows.quantity: b-value of magnitude-frequency distribution up to the largest observed event
rows.source: Sornette, Knopoff, Kagan & Vanneste (1996), Journal of Geophysical Research
rows.quote: for this catalog, b = 1.00 ± 0.02 up to the largest magnitude observed, MW ≃ 7.5
rows.notes: Regional b-value. Authors conclude seismogenic-layer thickness has no observable influence on the frequency distribution in this region.
rows.convention: cumulative magnitude-frequency, log10 N(>=M) = a - bM
rows.alternative_test: Single power law vs two-branch / roll-off forms: 'no evidence' for two branches or a needed roll-off in southern California (rank-ordering statistics). No log-normal comparison.

rows.item: Gutenberg-Richter b-value, spatiotemporal variability (literature review)
rows.quantity: range of reported b-values in the literature
rows.value_text: 0.3 <= b <= 2.5 (search snippet; long-term average 'close to unity')
rows.source: El-Isa & Eaton (2014), Tectonophysics
rows.quote: wide-ranging b-variations (0.3 <= b <= 2.5) have been reported in the literature
rows.notes: Abstract not retrievable (Elsevier; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex abstracts elided; Peeref page redirected). Range seen only in a search-engine excerpt; verify against the paper before use.
rows.convention: cumulative magnitude-frequency, log10 N(>=M) = a - bM

rows.item: Omori-Utsu aftershock decay exponent, worldwide compilation
rows.quantity: p-value of modified Omori law across >200 published estimates in >=50 papers
rows.value_text: distributed from 0.6 to 2.5 with a median of about 1.1 (abstract: usually p = 0.9-1.5)
rows.source: Utsu, Ogata & Matsu'ura (1995), Journal of Physics of the Earth
rows.quote: They are distributed from 0.6 to 2.5 with a median of about 1.1.
rows.notes: Section 3.2, compilation over the 33 years before 1995. No systematic dependence of p on mainshock magnitude or cut-off magnitude found.
rows.convention: modified Omori (Omori-Utsu) rate n(t) = K (t + c)^-p
rows.alternative_test: Section 12 reports Kisslinger (1993): stretched exponential vs modified Omori by AIC for 29 sequences (mostly California): Omori fits better in most cases with Ts = 0; with Ts > 0 the stretched exponential was better for about half. Utsu (unpublished 1992) Omori x exponential factor: exponential term went to zero.

rows.item: Omori-Utsu aftershock decay exponent, southern California (39 sequences)
rows.quantity: p-value of modified Omori law, maximum-likelihood estimates
rows.value_text: scatter from 0.7 to 1.8 with a mean of 1.11 ± 0.25
rows.source: Utsu, Ogata & Matsu'ura (1995), Journal of Physics of the Earth
rows.quote: The p values scatter from 0.7 to 1.8 with a mean of 1.11 + 0.25.
rows.notes: Kisslinger & Jones (1991) as summarized by Utsu et al. (1995), section 7 (regional variation); '+' in the extracted text is the ± sign. High p in Salton Trough (high heat flow).
rows.convention: modified Omori (Omori-Utsu) rate n(t) = K (t + c)^-p

rows.item: Landslide area, three event inventories (Northridge 1994, Umbria 1997, Hurricane Mitch Guatemala 1998)
rows.quantity: power-law tail exponent of the three-parameter inverse-gamma landslide-area PDF
rows.source: Malamud, Turcotte, Guzzetti & Reichenbach (2004), Earth Surface Processes and Landforms
rows.quote: for medium and large landslide areas decays as a power‐law with exponent ‐2·40
rows.notes: Same inverse-gamma fits all three inventories; exponential roll-over at small areas. Rockfall-dominated inventories differ substantially (Guzzetti 2006 dissertation reports Malamud et al. 2004 rockfall volume slope alpha+1 = 1.07, secondary).
rows.convention: non-cumulative probability density p(A_L) ~ A_L^-2.40 in the tail of an inverse-gamma distribution (sign as stated by the source)
rows.alternative_test: Abstract reports an inverse-gamma fit with power-law tail; no comparison against log-normal or other heavy-tailed forms stated in the abstract (full text not accessible: Durham repository behind a bot challenge).

rows.item: Landslide area, central Italy (Umbria-Marche reconnaissance inventory, 16,809; snowmelt event 1997, 4,233)
rows.quantity: exponent of non-cumulative frequency-area power-law fit
rows.value_text: exponent −2.5 for both data sets (0.03-4 km^2 and 0.001-0.1 km^2 ranges)
rows.source: Guzzetti, Malamud, Turcotte & Reichenbach (2002), Earth and Planetary Science Letters
rows.quote: The noncumulative frequency–area distribution of these landslides correlates well with a power-law relation, exponent −2.5
rows.notes: Roll-over at small areas attributed to incompleteness for data set A and judged real for data set B. Fit by regression on binned densities.
rows.convention: non-cumulative frequency density dN/dA_L ~ A_L^-2.5 (sign as stated)

rows.item: Landslide area, Taiwan and New Zealand inventories
rows.quantity: power-law tail exponent of the five-parameter double-Pareto landslide-area distribution
rows.source: Stark & Hovius (2001), Geophysical Research Letters, as reported in Guzzetti (2006), PhD dissertation ch. 5 'Statistics of landslide size'
rows.quote: obtained estimates for the slope of the power law tail of the distribution of α+1 = 2.11 for the Taiwan inventory, and α+1 = 2.46±0.2
rows.notes: Numbers checked in the secondary source (Guzzetti dissertation, full text); primary GRL abstract read via OpenAlex but it gives no number. Same dissertation shows model dependence: Staffora basin tail alpha+1 = 2.50 (double Pareto) vs 2.77 (inverse gamma); Umbria 1997 2.25 vs 2.33.
rows.convention: non-cumulative PDF tail exponent, p(A_L) ~ A_L^-(alpha+1); Guzzetti uses alpha for the cumulative exponent
rows.alternative_test: Abstract: simple power law does not fit most mapped landslides; double Pareto (two power-law regimes with a resolution-set crossover) proposed instead. No log-normal test reported in what was read.

rows.item: Rockfall volume on subvertical cliffs (Grenoble, Yosemite, worldwide catalogs)
rows.quantity: exponent b of the cumulative rockfall volume distribution
rows.value_text: 0.5 ± 0.2 (vs 1.2 ± 0.3 for mixed landslide types); Grenoble b ≈ 0.40 ± 0.06
rows.source: Dussauge, Grasso & Helmstetter (2003), Journal of Geophysical Research
rows.quote: the exponent values of rockfall volume on subvertical cliffs, 0.5 ± 0.2, is significantly smaller than the 1.2 ± 0.3 value
rows.notes: Volume range 10^2-10^10 m^3 across catalogs; Grenoble fit on 55 events above 40 m^3. Small samples.
rows.convention: cumulative N(V) ~ V^-b, N = number of events with volume greater than V
rows.alternative_test: Chi-square goodness of fit (5-18 bins): power law accepted at 95% for Grenoble; exponential, Weibull and Gumbel rejected over the same volume range. No log-normal test.

rows.item: Flood peak discharge, partial-duration series at six USGS stations (41-95,300 km^2, 74-110 yr)
rows.quantity: exponent a of discharge vs recurrence interval
rows.source: Malamud & Turcotte (2006), Journal of Hydrology
rows.quote: the power-law exponent a ranging from 0.27 to 0.90
rows.notes: Abstract text renders the relation as 'QwT a' (extraction artifact for Q ∝ T^a). Annual-maximum series argued to bias estimates.
rows.convention: Q_T ~ T^a, discharge Q associated with recurrence interval T (partial-duration series); not a PDF exponent
rows.alternative_test: Abstract reports power-law extrapolation checked against paleoflood estimates (within half an order of magnitude) and against the cumulative distribution of daily mean flows; no formal test vs GEV or log-Pearson III stated in the abstract.

rows.item: Fault / fracture length distribution (review)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of fracture length distribution
rows.source: Bonnet, Bour, Odling, Davy, Main, Cowie & Berkowitz (2001), Reviews of Geophysics
rows.notes: Full text blocked (Wiley and CORE returned 403/bot pages). Abstract says length, displacement and aperture exponents show wide variation 'frequently spanning the theoretically possible range' and that uncritical analysis has produced 'inaccurate and even meaningless exponents'. No numeric range recorded.
rows.convention: not established from text read (density n(l) ~ l^-a is the usual form in this literature; not verified in Bonnet et al.)
rows.alternative_test: Abstract notes some fracture systems are best described by scale-limited laws (lognormal, exponential); no per-data-set test result read.

rows.item: Hack's law, Virginia and Maryland streams (original)
rows.quantity: exponent of stream length vs drainage area
rows.value_text: L = 1.4 A^0.6 (coefficient averages about 1.4, ranges 1 to 2.5)
rows.units: dimensionless (L in miles, A in square miles)
rows.source: Hack (1957), USGS Professional Paper 294-B
rows.quote: Stream lengths tend to increase proportionally to the 0.6 power of the drainage area
rows.notes: Eq. (3) L = 1.4 A^0.6 is OCR-garbled in the scan but the 0.6 power is stated repeatedly in text. Regression-based, no uncertainty given.
rows.convention: Hack's law L ~ A^h, L = length of longest channel above a point, A = drainage area at that point

rows.item: Hack's exponent, real river networks (compilation)
rows.quantity: Hack exponent h over a reasonable span of basin sizes
rows.source: Dodds & Rothman (1999), Physical Review E, citing Maritan et al. (1996), Phys. Rev. E 53, 1510 (doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.53.1510)
rows.quote: it has been observed that for a reasonable span of basin sizes that 0.57 < h < 0.60
rows.notes: Dodds & Rothman cite refs [5, 9, 29, 30] incl. Maritan et al. 1996; Table II attributes 0.57-0.60 to Maritan et al. Very large basins may show h = 1/2. Rigon et al. (1996, WRR, doi 10.1029/96WR02397) abstract read but gives no number; full text blocked (403).
rows.convention: Hack's law l ~ a^h, l = main stream length, a = basin area

rows.item: Drainage (contributing) area distribution, real river networks
rows.quantity: exponent tau of the probability distribution of basin areas
rows.source: Dodds & Rothman (1999), Physical Review E, citing Maritan et al. (1996), Phys. Rev. E 53, 1510 (doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.53.1510)
rows.notes: Table II row, ref [9] = Maritan et al. (1996). The often-quoted exceedance exponent P[A >= a] ~ a^-beta is a different convention; not converted. Dodds & Rothman derive tau = 2 - h.
rows.convention: PDF/histogram exponent, P(a) ~ a^-tau (Dodds & Rothman eq. 4); 4/3 is the Scheidegger-model value

rows.item: Explosive volcanic eruption size, VEI >= 3 (global eruption databases)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of relative eruption frequency vs erupted volume
rows.source: Papale (2018), Scientific Reports
rows.quote: The computed power law exponent is 1.95, with p-value = 0.65 providing statistical robustness to the power law hypothesis
rows.notes: Fit is to Monte Carlo-derived relative frequencies of a handful of VEI classes (p-value computed with 533-variate synthetic samples), not to individual eruption volumes. Author notes k < 2 implies undefined mean.
rows.convention: F(x) = alpha x^-k, relative frequency of eruptions per VEI class vs erupted volume x (binned, VEI classes)
rows.alternative_test: Clauset-style xmin selection and KS goodness-of-fit only (power law not rejected, p = 0.65); no likelihood-ratio comparison with log-normal or tapered forms.

rows.item: Large explosive eruption magnitude-frequency, Holocene global database (M >= 4)
rows.quantity: power-law / tail exponent of eruption magnitude-frequency
rows.source: Deligne, Coles & Sparks (2010), Journal of Geophysical Research
rows.notes: Abstract: EVT magnitude-frequency robust up to M = 7; extrapolation to M > 8 inconsistent with geology (e.g. Fish Canyon Tuff), read as different mechanisms above M 7. No exponent in abstract; full text closed. Pyle and Simkin & Siebert VEI-frequency values not searched to completion.
rows.convention: not established (extreme value theory model; parameters not in abstract)
rows.alternative_test: Extreme value theory with and without under-reporting correction; no power-law vs alternative comparison stated in abstract.

rows.item: Wildfire burned area, USA and Australia (incl. paleo-fire records)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of burned-area distribution
rows.value_text: beta ranging from 1.3 to 1.5 (Malamud et al. 2005, 18 US ecoregions: 1.3 to 1.75)
rows.source: Malamud, Morein & Turcotte (1998), Science, as reported in Corral & Gonzalez (2019), Earth and Space Science
rows.quote: follow (untruncated) power-law distributions with exponent β ranging from 1.3 to 1.5
rows.notes: Number checked in Corral & Gonzalez (2019) full text (arXiv 1810.07868), section 4.3; Malamud 1998 Science abstract (Semantic Scholar) read: states 'power-law frequency-area statistics over many orders of magnitude' but gives no number. Corral reports the exponents in its PDF-beta convention; Malamud's original is a non-cumulative frequency-area slope.
rows.convention: PDF exponent beta, f(x) ~ x^-beta (Corral eq. 1; CCDF exponent would be beta-1, not used here)
rows.alternative_test: None in Malamud et al. (1998) as reported; Corral notes later authors found log-normal better in other regions (Corral et al. 2008; Hantson et al. 2016).

rows.item: Wildfire burned area, Angola (Landsat, 4 years)
rows.quantity: PDF exponent of untruncated power-law tail of burned area
rows.value_text: beta = 1.818 above 63 ha (p 0.22, n 1,294, 3.63 decades); bootstrap 1.79 ± 0.07
rows.source: Corral & Gonzalez (2019), Earth and Space Science
rows.notes: Table 1 and section 4.3. Truncated log-normal (Table 3) fits from 8.7 ha over 4.49 decades with n = 5,349, about 4x more data than the power law. Preferred: truncated log-normal (Table 6). Data from Hantson et al. (2016).
rows.convention: PDF exponent beta, f(x) ~ x^-beta (Corral eq. 1; CCDF exponent would be beta-1, not used here)
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: cv_l test power law vs truncated log-normal: power law not rejected over its range, but log-normal valid over a much larger range; Table 6 prefers truncated log-normal.

rows.item: Wildfire burned area, Canada boreal forest (Landsat, 14 years)
rows.quantity: PDF exponent of truncated power-law regime of burned area
rows.value_text: truncated power law beta = 1.153 for 1.0-12,600 ha (p 0.23, n 395); bootstrap 1.21 ± 0.08
rows.source: Corral & Gonzalez (2019), Earth and Space Science
rows.notes: Table 4. Only 408 fires. Table 6: 'truncated power law + truncated log-normal' with no clear transition between them. Hantson et al. (2016) original: truncated power law exponent 1.0 for Canada.
rows.convention: PDF exponent beta, f(x) ~ x^-beta (Corral eq. 1; CCDF exponent would be beta-1, not used here)
rows.alternative_test: Truncated power law vs untruncated vs truncated log-normal (cv_l test, KS p-values): both a truncated power-law regime and a log-normal covering the largest fires are acceptable.

rows.item: Wildfire size, US federal land 1986-1996 (Clauset data set o)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of tail of fire size (acres)
rows.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), SIAM Review
rows.notes: Table 6.1: n = 203 785, xmin 6324 ± 3487 acres, ntail 521 ± 6801, power-law GOF p = 0.05 (ruled out under p <= 0.1). Data-set list says US federal land 1986-1996, Fig. 6.1 caption says California forest fires: inconsistency inside the source. Exponent is far from Malamud's 1.3-1.5 (different data, method and convention).
rows.convention: PDF exponent alpha, p(x) ~ x^-alpha for x >= xmin (Clauset eq. 1.1); fitted by maximum likelihood with xmin chosen by minimizing KS distance; '1.64(4)' means 1.64 +/- 0.04
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Vuong LR (Table 6.2): log-normal -1.78 (p 0.08), exponential 4.00 (p 0.00), stretched exp. -1.82 (p 0.07); nested LR vs power law + cut-off -5.02 (p 0.00). Verdict 'with cut-off'.

rows.item: Solar flare peak gamma-ray intensity 1980-1989 (Clauset data set p; heliophysics, kept per task scope)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of tail of flare peak intensity
rows.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), SIAM Review
rows.notes: Heliophysics, not geoscience; moved to comparison on 2026-10-30. Table 6.1: power-law GOF p = 1.00 (plausible), yet cut-off form favored by LR. Space-physics observable, not solid-Earth.
rows.convention: PDF exponent alpha, p(x) ~ x^-alpha for x >= xmin (Clauset eq. 1.1); fitted by maximum likelihood with xmin chosen by minimizing KS distance; '1.64(4)' means 1.64 +/- 0.04
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Vuong LR (Table 6.2): log-normal -0.803 (p 0.42), exponential 13.7 (p 0.00), stretched exp. -0.546 (p 0.59); nested LR vs power law + cut-off -4.52 (p 0.00). Verdict 'with cut-off'.

rows.item: Tropical cyclone power dissipation index (PDI), North Atlantic + Northeast Pacific
rows.quantity: PDF exponent of truncated power-law regime of PDI
rows.source: Corral & Gonzalez (2019), Earth and Space Science
rows.quote: an exponent β in the range 1.1–1.2, for about 2 orders of magnitude
rows.notes: Tables 4-6. Separate basins: NAtl 1.224, EPac 1.085. Untruncated fits to the extreme tail give steep, poorly constrained exponents (3.3-5.1) over < 1 decade. Agrees with Corral, Osso & Llebot (2010, Nature Physics), not read.
rows.convention: PDF exponent beta, f(x) ~ x^-beta (Corral eq. 1; CCDF exponent would be beta-1, not used here)
rows.alternative_test: Truncated power law preferred (Table 6); truncated log-normal with no upper cut-off does not fit; log-normal not preferred for the tail.

rows.item: Tsunami run-up heights, ten locations in Japan (NGDC data)
rows.quantity: exponent of cumulative frequency-size distribution of run-up height
rows.source: Burroughs & Tebbens (2005), Pure and Applied Geophysics
rows.notes: Snippet: a power law or upper-truncated power law describes the cumulative run-up distribution at all ten locations; per-site exponents not seen. Abstract not available via Semantic Scholar or OpenAlex.
rows.convention: cumulative frequency-size (exact form not verified)
rows.alternative_test: Power law vs upper-truncated power law per site (from snippet only).

rows.item: Coastline / frontier fractal dimension (Richardson's divider data)
rows.quantity: fractional (fractal) dimension D from length vs measuring-step scaling
rows.value_text: D = 1.25 west coast of Britain; 1.15 German land frontier (c. 1899); 1.14 Spain-Portugal; 1.13 Australian coast; 1.02 South Africa
rows.source: Mandelbrot (1967), Science
rows.quote: I propose to interpret them as implying, for example, that the dimension of the west coast of Great Britain is D = 1.25.
rows.notes: Values are Mandelbrot's reinterpretation of Richardson's empirical slopes; read from a JSTOR scan hosted by Humboldt State. No uncertainty or fitting range given.
rows.convention: divider length L(G) ~ G^(1-D) for step length G; log-log slope magnitude D-1

rows.item: Frequency of word use, Moby Dick (Clauset data set a)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of the distribution tail
rows.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), SIAM Review
rows.notes: Table 6.1 row. GOF p = 0.49.
rows.convention: PDF exponent alpha, p(x) ~ x^-alpha for x >= xmin (Clauset eq. 1.1); fitted by maximum likelihood with xmin chosen by minimizing KS distance; '1.64(4)' means 1.64 +/- 0.04
rows.alternative_test: Table 6.3 (discrete): Poisson 4.43 (p 0.00), log-normal 0.395 (p 0.69), exponential 9.09 (p 0.00), stretched exp. 4.13 (p 0.00), cut-off -0.899 (p 0.18). Verdict 'good': the only data set of 24 rated good.

rows.item: Population of US cities, 2000 Census (Clauset data set m)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of the distribution tail
rows.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), SIAM Review
rows.notes: Table 6.1 row. GOF p = 0.76.
rows.convention: PDF exponent alpha, p(x) ~ x^-alpha for x >= xmin (Clauset eq. 1.1); fitted by maximum likelihood with xmin chosen by minimizing KS distance; '1.64(4)' means 1.64 +/- 0.04
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Table 6.2: log-normal -0.090 (p 0.93), exponential 3.65 (p 0.00), stretched exp. 0.204 (p 0.84), cut-off -0.123 (p 0.62). Verdict 'moderate': power law plausible but log-normal and stretched exponential equally plausible.

rows.item: Citations to papers published 1981 (Science Citation Index; Clauset data set u)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of the distribution tail
rows.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), SIAM Review
rows.notes: Table 6.1 row. GOF p = 0.20. Clauset notes earlier ad hoc estimates of 2.9 and 2.5 for the same data are incompatible with 3.16 ± 0.06.
rows.convention: PDF exponent alpha, p(x) ~ x^-alpha for x >= xmin (Clauset eq. 1.1); fitted by maximum likelihood with xmin chosen by minimizing KS distance; '1.64(4)' means 1.64 +/- 0.04
rows.tested_vs_alternatives: tested, alternative favored or not distinguishable
rows.alternative_test: Table 6.3: Poisson 6.54 (p 0.00), log-normal -0.141 (p 0.89), exponential 5.91 (p 0.00), stretched exp. 1.72 (p 0.09), cut-off -0.007 (p 0.91). Verdict 'moderate'.

rows.item: Hits to web sites, AOL users, one day (Clauset data set w)
rows.quantity: power-law exponent of the distribution tail

rows.notes: Remaining 7 ruled out: HTTP connections, earthquakes, web links, fires, wealth, web hits, metabolic network. Only word frequencies rated 'good' (no plausible alternative).
